outcome: No source I could reach reports the conjecture settled, disproved or refuted as of 13 Oct 2026. Two events since 26 Jan 2024 bear on it: a restricted-class result for contractible cellular fake surfaces of complexity less than 6 (Fagan, Qiu and Wang, first posted 16 Dec 2024, revised 8 Jan 2026), and a reduction of the general case to standard polyhedra (Dynnikov, arXiv 24 Aug 2026). Neither settles the conjecture as stated.
problem_asks: One universal yes/no question with no separate parts. For every finite contractible two-dimensional CW complex K, is the product K x [0,1] collapsible? Terms as the statement gives them: finite, contractible, two-dimensional CW complex, the closed unit interval, and collapsible (to a point). The statement does not say whether collapsible refers to the product's given cell structure or to a subdivision of it. The literature states both forms (Zeeman's original in polyhedra; Adiprasito and Benedetti's subdivided form, which Wikipedia calls an equivalent restatement), so a result on either form bears on the question. The statement does not name a subclass, so a result on a subclass answers only part of it.

events.what_happened: Ikeda, 'acyclic fake surfaces that are spines of 3-manifolds', Osaka J. Math. 9(3) (1972), 391-408. Per secondary descriptions (a search summary of Ikeda's paper, and the Fagan-Qiu-Wang reference list), it characterises one class of acyclic closed fake surfaces geometrically and shows Zeeman's conjecture holds for every member of that class. The scanned PDF had no extractable text, so the class and the exact claim are unverified.
events.delivers: Zeeman's conjecture for the members of one class of acyclic closed fake surfaces (the exact class is not read). A restricted case, per the secondary descriptions.
events.remains: Zeeman's conjecture for all contractible two-dimensional polyhedra outside that class, which is nearly all of the problem.

checked_by.who: Osaka Journal of Mathematics (refereed journal of record)

events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for the class described.

events.what_happened: S. A. Popov, 1972, Russian journal (mathnet record sm3235; not opened, server returned 503). Per search summaries, Popov constructs PL embeddings in R^4 of a class of two-dimensional polyhedra, including the dunce hat and related polyhedra, whose complements are not simply connected, and so refutes a claim called a 'Zeeman conjecture' about embeddings. This is a different statement that shares the name.
events.delivers: Refutes an embedding claim (that every PL embedding of the dunce hat in R^4 has simply connected complement, per summaries). It says nothing about whether K x [0,1] is collapsible.
events.remains: The whole of the collapsibility conjecture.

checked_by.who: Russian journal of record (identified from the mathnet record)

events.direction: Refutes a different (embedding) statement that carries the same name. Does not bear on the collapsibility conjecture.
events.object: Per summaries only: linear embeddings in R^4 of a class of two-dimensional polyhedra (dunce-hat-type, contractible but not combinatorially contractible) with non-simply-connected complements. Whether the embeddings are explicit is not established.

events.what_happened: M. Cohen, 'Dimension estimates in collapsing X x I^q', Topology 14 (1975), 253-256. The citation is confirmed by a 1983 Canadian J. Math. reference; the paper itself was not opened. Reported content, via a search summary of a later paper: for every contractible 2-complex C, the product C x I^q is PL equivalent to a collapsible complex, so that some subdivision of C x I^q is collapsible; one source gives q = 6, another gives q = 5 and makes it conditional on the four-dimensional Poincare conjecture (later proved by Freedman). The exponent is in dispute.
events.delivers: A weaker statement than the conjecture: a product with I^q for some q (5 or 6 per the sources) is collapsible, for every contractible 2-complex. It does not give K x [0,1], since q is greater than 1.
events.remains: The conjecture itself, which is the case q = 1.
events.direction: A weaker form, consistent with the conjecture. It does not move the conjecture.

events.what_happened: M. Cohen, 1977, reported by a search summary of the Encyclopedia of Mathematics 'Collapsibility' article: the extended collapsibility statement is shown to be false beyond dimension 2. The Encyclopedia page was unreachable (502 on three attempts). The 1977 paper was not located, so this is unverified. A search summary also reports that for every d > 2 there is a contractible d-complex whose product with a single interval has no collapsible subdivision.
events.delivers: A higher-dimensional analogue fails: for d greater than 2 there is a contractible d-complex whose product with an interval has no collapsible subdivision (per the summary). It concerns complexes of dimension three and above.
events.remains: Nothing of the two-dimensional conjecture. This is a different question.
events.direction: Different question (higher-dimensional analogue). It does not bear on the two-dimensional case.
events.object: Per summary only: a contractible d-complex for each d greater than 2 whose product with an interval has no collapsible subdivision. Not described in enough detail to say whether it is explicit.

events.what_happened: D. Gillman and D. Rolfsen, 'The Zeeman conjecture for standard spines is equivalent to the Poincare conjecture', Topology 22(3) (1983), 315-323, DOI 10.1016/0040-9383(83)90017-4. The publisher page only redirected, so the body was not read. Per the title and secondary descriptions (the Matveev-Rolfsen 1993 chapter, and the Dartmouth seminar abstract of 6 Nov 2025), the conjecture restricted to standard spines of 3-manifolds is equivalent to the Poincare conjecture.
events.delivers: Equivalence: the conjecture restricted to standard spines of 3-manifolds holds if and only if the Poincare conjecture does. A restricted class.
events.remains: The conjecture for every other contractible two-dimensional polyhedron, namely non-standard polyhedra and polyhedra that are not spines of 3-manifolds.

checked_by.who: D. Gillman and D. Rolfsen (authors); Topology, Elsevier (refereed journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: Authors work in low-dimensional topology; journal publication is refereed

events.direction: Reduces the restricted conjecture to the Poincare conjecture. The Poincare conjecture is now proved (Perelman), so the restricted case holds.

events.what_happened: S. V. Matveev, 'Transformations of special spines and the Zeeman conjecture', Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat. 51:5 (1987), 1104-1116; Math. USSR-Izv. 31:2 (1988), 423-434, DOI 10.1070/IM1988v031n02ABEH001083 (received 17 Oct 1985). Per a search summary, it defines two elementary transformations of special spines, shows that any two special spines of a 3-manifold are related by them, and applies this to the Zeeman conjecture for 1-collapsibility of contractible two-dimensional polyhedra. The mathnet page returned 503, so the statement it proves about the conjecture was not read.
events.delivers: Not established from my reading. Per the summary, a special-spine transformation theorem for 3-manifolds, applied to the conjecture for special spines. The exact polyhedra covered, and whether any case is settled, are not known to me.
events.remains: The conjecture in general, and any residual cases of the special-spine application that I could not read.

checked_by.who: Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya (refereed journal of record); author S. V. Matveev

events.direction: Not established from the sources I could read. The summary describes it as bearing on the conjecture for special spines.

events.what_happened: S. V. Matveev, 'The Zeeman conjecture for nonthickenable special polyhedra is equivalent to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture', Sibirsk. Mat. Zh. 28:6 (1987), 66-80; Siberian Math. J. 28:6 (1987), 917-928, DOI 10.1007/BF00969470. The title is as cited in search results; the paper was not opened. The Dartmouth seminar abstract paraphrases the same work as: for standard polyhedra that are not spines of 3-manifolds, the conjecture is equivalent to a weakened Andrews-Curtis conjecture. A search summary of Matveev's results instead says the restriction to special polyhedra is equivalent to the union of the Poincare and Andrews-Curtis conjectures. The paraphrases differ; see disputes.
events.delivers: Per the title: for nonthickenable special polyhedra, the conjecture is equivalent to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture. An equivalence restricted to nonthickenable special polyhedra. It settles neither conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture for thickenable special polyhedra and for non-special polyhedra; the Andrews-Curtis conjecture itself.

checked_by.who: Siberian Mathematical Journal (refereed journal of record); author S. V. Matveev

events.direction: An equivalence, restricted to nonthickenable special polyhedra. It does not decide either side.

events.what_happened: Chapter XI, 'Zeeman's Collapsing Conjecture', by S. Matveev and D. Rolfsen, in C. Hog-Angeloni, W. Metzler and A. J. Sieradski (eds.), Two-Dimensional Homotopy and Combinatorial Group Theory, Cambridge University Press, 1993, pp. 335-364 (online 20 Jan 2010). A survey, with no new result claimed. It records the statement (Z) and its status: '(Z) has not been refuted (if it is false!)', and 'we have no methods of detecting non-collapsibility for contractible 3-dimensional polyhedra of the form P2 x I'. It credits the first contributions to special cases to P. Dierker, W. B. R. Lickorish and D. Gillman.
events.delivers: No new result. A status record: as of 1993 the conjecture was neither proved nor refuted, special cases had been proved, and weakened versions had been proved and strengthened versions disproved.

checked_by.who: S. Matveev and D. Rolfsen (authors); Cambridge University Press (book)
checked_by.qualification: Experts in 3-manifold and two-complex topology writing a survey
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote the survey and its status summary

events.direction: No direction. It records status only.

events.what_happened: G. Perelman, 'The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications', arXiv:math/0211159, submitted 11 Nov 2002, one version (v1, 39 pages). This is the first of Perelman's preprints on the Poincare conjecture; the argument is completed in two later 2003 preprints that I did not open. Its bearing on this problem is indirect: by Gillman and Rolfsen (1983), the conjecture restricted to standard spines of 3-manifolds is equivalent to the Poincare conjecture. The first sentence of the abstract was read; I did not see a mention of the Zeeman conjecture in what I read.
events.delivers: Through Gillman and Rolfsen: the conjecture holds for standard spines of 3-manifolds, a restricted class. The preprint does not itself prove anything about the collapsibility conjecture, as far as I read.
events.remains: The conjecture for every contractible two-dimensional polyhedron outside that restricted class, which is nearly all of it.
events.direction: Proves the Poincare conjecture, which by Gillman and Rolfsen makes the conjecture true for standard spines of 3-manifolds. Cuts toward the conjecture in that restricted case.

events.what_happened: K. Adiprasito and B. Benedetti, 'Subdivisions, shellability, and collapsibility of products', arXiv:1202.6606. Versions: v1 29 Feb 2012; v2 8 Apr 2012; v3 10 Jul 2013, described as 'Entirely rewritten version'. Read from the ar5iv render of the latest version. Results read: (i) a PL characterisation of spheres and balls by shellability after derived subdivisions; (ii) Theorem D / Corollary II.1.6: for any contractible complex C there is n >= 0 with C x I^n collapsible; (iii) Section II.2: the number of subdivisions needed for collapsibility cannot be bounded. The text states 'The Zeeman conjecture claims that the product of any contractible 2-dimensional complex C with the interval [0,1] is PL homeomorphic to a collapsible complex' and 'To this day the Zeeman conjecture remains open'. Wikipedia cites this paper for the subdivided restatement of the conjecture; I did not see that equivalence sentence verbatim.
events.revisions: v1 29 Feb 2012; v2 8 Apr 2012; v3 10 Jul 2013 ('Entirely rewritten version'). The 'remains open' sentence is in the latest version read, so it dates from 2013 or later.
events.delivers: A reformulation: per Wikipedia's citation, the conjecture is equivalent to 'for every contractible 2-complex C, some barycentric subdivision of C x I is collapsible'. Also: for each contractible C some C x I^n is collapsible, with n not fixed at 1, a weaker statement; and no uniform subdivision count works. None of this settles the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture itself: the case n = 1, with or without subdivision.
events.direction: Reformulates the conjecture and proves weaker product statements plus an unbounded subdivision count. Neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture.
events.object: The paper's Theorem II.2.7, as fetched: 'there is a 3-ball B such that sd^m(B x I^n) is not collapsible', for any m, n >= 0. The introduction describes a contractible 2-complex C_{m,n} with sd^m(C_{m,n} x I^n) not collapsible. Whether the construction is explicit is not established from what I read.

events.what_happened: L. Fagan, Y. Qiu and Z. Wang, 'Classification of Cellular Fake Surfaces', arXiv:2406.09439. Versions: v1 11 Jun 2024; v2 18 Jul 2024; v3 8 Jan 2026. The abstract classifies acyclic cellular fake surfaces up to complexity 4 and those without small disks at complexity 5, and proves the contractibility conjecture at complexity 4 and the embedded-disk conjecture up to complexity 5. Its abstract names the Zeeman conjecture as motivation ('especially the Andrews-Curtis and Zeeman conjectures'). The journal listing gives Journal of Experimental Mathematics 2(1) (2026), paper 6; I did not open the listing.
events.revisions: v1 11 Jun 2024; v2 18 Jul 2024; v3 8 Jan 2026. Journal of Experimental Mathematics 2(1) (2026) per listing.
events.delivers: Classification of acyclic cellular fake surfaces at complexity up to 4, partial at 5, and the contractibility conjecture for acyclic fake surfaces of complexity 4. A different conjecture, about acyclic fake surfaces. It is tooling in the same programme but not the collapsibility conjecture.

checked_by.who: Journal of Experimental Mathematics (per the journal listing)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the classification (listing only; not opened)

events.direction: A different question. It says nothing about whether the conjecture is true.

events.what_happened: A. Shehper, A. M. Medina-Mardones, L. Fagan, B. Lewandowski, A. Gruen, Y. Qiu, P. Kucharski, Z. Wang and S. Gukov, 'What makes math problems hard for reinforcement learning: a case study', arXiv:2408.15332. Submitted 27 Aug 2024; revised 11 Feb 2025; accepted to NeurIPS 2025. The Andrews-Curtis conjecture is used as a reinforcement-learning environment. The paper reports length reducibility of all but two Akbulut-Kirby presentations (1981), and resolution of Miller-Schupp potential counterexamples, including three infinite subfamilies. The abstract page names no AI system. Its reinforcement-learning agent is unnamed. A search summary says the paper has a language-modelling component; I did not verify that in the paper.
events.revisions: v1 27 Aug 2024 (a different author list per a search summary); v2 11 Feb 2025 (nine authors); NeurIPS 2025 version.
events.delivers: For the Andrews-Curtis conjecture, not the collapsibility conjecture: length reduction for the Akbulut-Kirby series (all but two) and for Miller-Schupp families, eliminating candidate counterexamples to the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture for those presentations. Nothing for the collapsibility conjecture.
events.remains: The whole collapsibility conjecture. The Andrews-Curtis conjecture itself remains open per the abstract.

checked_by.who: NeurIPS 2025 (peer-reviewed conference; acceptance per a search summary, paper not opened)
checked_by.qualification: Machine-learning conference refereeing, not topology refereeing

events.direction: For the Andrews-Curtis conjecture: eliminates candidate counterexamples for those presentations, consistent with the conjecture. No bearing on the collapsibility conjecture.
events.object: Explicit stable Andrews-Curtis trivialisation sequences for the Akbulut-Kirby and Miller-Schupp presentations, produced by the reinforcement-learning search and listed in a code repository (the arXiv comments name a repository containing 'AC-Solver'). Constructive: each claimed presentation comes with an explicit move sequence.

events.what_happened: L. Fagan, Y. Qiu and Z. Wang, 'Stable Andrews-Curtis Conjecture via Fake Surfaces and Zeeman Conjecture', arXiv:2412.12293. v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jan 2026 (the current version). The paper proposes an induction scheme for the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture (sACC), which is equivalent to 'every contractible fake surface is 3-deformable to a point'. Theorem 1 (v2): 'Contractible fake surfaces of complexity less than 6 with connected 1-skeletons are all 3-deformable to a point.' Corollary 4 (v2, Introduction): 'The Zeeman conjecture holds for any contractible cellular fake surface F of complexity less than 6.' The introduction also says: 'In the case of contractible fake surfaces that are not embeddable in 3-manifolds, the Zeeman conjecture is equivalent to sACC', and 'The Zeeman conjecture is believed to be false as well, but there are interesting special cases.' The v1 abstract, as fetched, makes no Zeeman claim (the title has 'Zeeman Conjecture'). Whether v1 already contains Corollary 4 is not verified.
events.revisions: v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jan 2026 (the current version). The changes between versions were not identified.
events.delivers: The conjecture for contractible cellular fake surfaces of complexity less than 6 (complexity read as vertex count, per the paper's ℱC(s,t) definition). A restricted class, not all contractible two-dimensional complexes. Also, per the authors, the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture for that complexity range.
events.remains: The conjecture for all contractible two-dimensional complexes outside that class: higher complexity, and complexes that are not fake surfaces. The stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture in general. Whether Corollary 4 carries the connected-1-skeleton hypothesis of Theorem 1 is not established.
events.time_since_posted: 22 months since v1 (Dec 2024); 9 months since v2 (Jan 2026)
events.directly_checkable: The objects are finite combinatorial complexes with at most five vertices, so the claims are finite checks in principle. Whether a computer check was used is not established from the sections I read; the paper says 'computer exploration has not yielded any new results so far'.
events.doubts: (1) Scope. The v2 abstract states the result without the connected-1-skeleton hypothesis that v2's Theorem 1 carries. Whether Corollary 4 inherits that hypothesis is not established from my reading. (2) The Zeeman claim is confined to cellular fake surfaces, while the conjecture concerns all finite contractible two-dimensional complexes. (3) The paper describes itself as 'an induction scheme that aims at establishing' sACC. Its proved part is the low-complexity case.
events.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture holding in the restricted class (the authors prove it there). The authors state that the Zeeman conjecture is 'believed to be false' in general, and that sACC is 'widely believed to be false'. That is their own belief, recorded here, not a verdict.

events.what_happened: A. Lisitsa, 'Stable Andrews-Curtis trivialization of AK(3) revisited. A case study using automated deduction', arXiv:2501.18601, submitted 17 Jan 2025. It gives an alternative certificate that the Akbulut-Kirby presentation AK(3) is stably Andrews-Curtis equivalent to the trivial presentation. The transformation sequences come from two proofs generated by the automated theorem prover Prover9. The abstract refers to a 2024 result by Shehper et al. Neither the Zeeman conjecture nor collapsibility is mentioned on the page read. Prover9 is a classical automated theorem prover, and the source does not call it AI.
events.delivers: Stable Andrews-Curtis equivalence of AK(3) to the trivial presentation, by an alternative proof. An Andrews-Curtis result, not the collapsibility conjecture.
events.remains: The collapsibility conjecture, and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture for other presentations.
events.directly_checkable: Explicit transformation sequences for AK(3), certifying the equivalence and checkable by hand move by move.
events.direction: For the Andrews-Curtis conjecture: confirms one presentation's stable trivialisation, which removes AK(3) as a candidate counterexample. No bearing on the collapsibility conjecture.
events.object: Explicit transformation sequences from AK(3) to the trivial presentation, generated by Prover9 and certifying the stable equivalence. Constructive.

events.what_happened: C. Zhang, A. Zhou, R. J. George, S. Gukov and Animashree Anandkumar, 'AI-Driven Mathematical Discovery for the Andrews-Curtis Conjecture', poster at the MATH-AI workshop, NeurIPS 2025, San Diego. The page is opened. It benchmarks LLM theorem provers on Andrews-Curtis tasks, formalises the conjecture in Lean with a deterministic autoformaliser ('ACC'), uses LLMs to synthesise reusable theorem statements from the generated Lean proofs, and feeds them to reinforcement-learning agent training. It reports 753 Miller-Schupp presentations solved, 'disproving them as potential counterexamples to the AC conjecture'. The page names no specific AI system ('LLMs', 'state-of-the-art LLM theorem provers'). The page gives no poster date.
events.delivers: For the Andrews-Curtis conjecture: 753 Miller-Schupp presentations ruled out as potential counterexamples. The abstract says the conjecture remains open. Nothing for the collapsibility conjecture.
events.remains: The collapsibility conjecture, and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture itself.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the work for poster presentation

machine_checked.system: Lean (autoformalised Andrews-Curtis trivialisations via the ACC autoformaliser)

events.directly_checkable: Trivialisation paths for the 753 presentations, each with a generated Lean proof. Not checked by me.
events.direction: For the Andrews-Curtis conjecture: rules out candidate counterexamples, consistent with the conjecture. No bearing on the collapsibility conjecture.
events.object: Explicit trivialisation paths for 753 Miller-Schupp presentations, each certified by an autoformalised Lean proof, per the abstract.

events.what_happened: M. Lackenby, 'The stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture and thickenable presentations of the trivial group', arXiv:2606.06122, submitted 4 Jun 2026. Per the abstract page read: an explicit upper bound on the number of stable Andrews-Curtis moves that convert a thickenable balanced presentation of the trivial group to the standard one-generator presentation, and a proof that thickenable balanced presentations satisfy the unstable Andrews-Curtis conjecture. The page does not mention the Zeeman conjecture, collapsibility, or AI. The full text was not read. I did not check whether thickenable presentation complexes fall under the three-manifold-embeddable case of Dynnikov's Theorem 1.5; that is a point for the judging pass.
events.delivers: Stable and unstable Andrews-Curtis results for thickenable balanced presentations of the trivial group. An explicit move bound. An Andrews-Curtis result for a class, not the collapsibility conjecture.
events.remains: The collapsibility conjecture, and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture for other presentations.
events.direction: For the Andrews-Curtis conjecture, in a class. It neither confirms nor refutes the collapsibility conjecture.

events.what_happened: I. Dynnikov, 'On Zeeman's collapsibility conjecture for non-standard polyhedra', arXiv:2608.23331, submitted 24 Aug 2026. One version (v1), 18 pages, 4 figures, math.GT, sole author. Abstract, verbatim: 'We prove that if Zeeman's collapsibility conjecture holds for standard polyhedra, then it holds in general.' Body (arXiv HTML, read via a summariser): Conjecture 1.1 is the collapsibility conjecture as stated. Theorem 1.4: if some compact contractible two-polyhedron K is not r-collapsible (K x [0,1]^r not collapsible) for some r in N, then some standard contractible two-polyhedron is not r-collapsible. Theorem 1.5: 'ZCC holds for polyhedra embeddable into three-manifolds.' Theorem 2.5: each contractible K is 3-deformable to a semi-standard polyhedron K' = K1 # ... # Km, with K' embeddable when K is, and K r-collapsible when each Ki is. Definition 2.1: standard means every non-vertex edge point has a theta-graph link and every vertex has a K4 link. The acknowledgements say 'Google Gemini (Web version) was used solely for the purpose of final language editing.' The same work was given as a Dartmouth Topology Seminar talk on 6 Nov 2025, 'On Zeeman's conjecture for non-standard polyhedra'. Per section 5.1 the event is dated to the write-up.
events.delivers: A reduction: the conjecture for all compact contractible two-polyhedra follows from the conjecture for standard polyhedra (Theorem 1.4 for each r). Also Theorem 1.5, the conjecture for polyhedra embeddable in three-manifolds, a restricted class. The talk abstract attributes that class to Gillman and Rolfsen with the Poincare conjecture; whether Dynnikov's proof is new is not established.
events.remains: The conjecture for standard two-polyhedra in general, including standard polyhedra not embeddable in 3-manifolds. Whether that residue is linked to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture (via Matveev) is not established by me.
events.direction: A reduction. It asserts neither that the conjecture holds nor that it fails. It moves the question to standard polyhedra.

disputes.summary: Matveev 1987 (nonthickenable special polyhedra). The title, as cited, says the conjecture for these polyhedra is equivalent to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture. The Dartmouth seminar abstract paraphrases the standard-polyhedra, non-3-manifold case as equivalent to a weakened Andrews-Curtis conjecture. A search summary of Matveev's results says the restriction to special polyhedra is equivalent to the union of the Poincare and Andrews-Curtis conjectures. These are three different wordings of one result, and the 1987 papers were not read.

Cohen 1975. One source reports C x I^6 PL-collapsible for every contractible 2-complex C. Another reports C x I^5, conditional on the four-dimensional Poincare conjecture, which Freedman later proved. The exponent is disputed and the 1975 paper was not read.

Adiprasito and Benedetti. The introduction describes a contractible 2-complex C_{m,n} with sd^m(C_{m,n} x I^n) not collapsible. Theorem II.2.7, as fetched, states the same for a 3-ball B. The subdivision count is unbounded either way; the discrepancy is in the type of object.

'Zeeman conjecture' names two different statements. One is the collapsibility conjecture. The other is the embedding claim about the dunce hat in R^4 and simply connected complements (Popov 1972). Not a priority dispute, but the same name is used for different questions.

summary: Searched 39 queries and opened the pages listed in sources: the arXiv abstracts and HTML for the 2024-2026 preprints, Wikipedia's Zeeman article (last edited 1 Oct 2025, which labels the problem an 'Unproven mathematical hypothesis' and cites only Adiprasito-Benedetti 2012 and Matveev 2007), the Dartmouth topology seminar page, the 1993 Cambridge chapter, the NeurIPS 2025 poster page, and ar5iv for Adiprasito-Benedetti. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics page and the mathnet pages returned 502 or 503 on repeated attempts, and the Gillman-Rolfsen and Ikeda papers could not be read; those claims rest on secondary descriptions and are marked as such. No source reports the conjecture resolved, disproved or refuted. The two post-2024 items are (1) Fagan, Qiu and Wang (arXiv 2412.12293, v1 16 Dec 2024, v2 8 Jan 2026), who prove the conjecture for contractible cellular fake surfaces of complexity less than 6 (Corollary 4) and say it is 'believed to be false' in general; and (2) Dynnikov (arXiv 2608.23331, 24 Aug 2026, one version), who proves that the conjecture for all contractible two-polyhedra follows from the conjecture for standard polyhedra, and also states that it holds for polyhedra embeddable in 3-manifolds (Theorem 1.5). Neither is a settlement. Where the call is close: (a) Fagan, Qiu and Wang is a real case of the conjecture, but a strict subclass that excludes non-fake-surface complexes, and its Theorem 1 carries a connected-1-skeleton hypothesis that the abstract omits; (b) Dynnikov moves the question without deciding it; (c) Adiprasito-Benedetti's product results (n not fixed at 1) are weaker than the conjecture and do not move it. Pre-2024 events that bear on the conjecture are restricted-case results: Gillman-Rolfsen 1983 (equivalence with the Poincare conjecture for standard spines of 3-manifolds), Perelman 2002 (which makes that restricted case true), Matveev 1987 (two papers), Adiprasito-Benedetti 2012, and Ikeda 1972, plus status records (Matveev and Rolfsen 1993: '(Z) has not been refuted'). AI: 39 searches, including explicit checks of lab announcements and AI-result trackers, found no AI system credited with any result on this conjecture. Dynnikov's acknowledgements credit 'Google Gemini (Web version)' with 'final language editing' only, which is recorded with none_found false and no systems. The AI-involved papers that came up concern the Andrews-Curtis conjecture (Shehper et al. 2024; Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2025, which name no specific model), and are recorded as discarded events because they answer a different question. Lisitsa 2025 uses the classical prover Prover9, which the source does not call AI. OpenAI's August 2026 Astra list has no topology item (opened the siliconangle report, not OpenAI's own page). Sra's 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (arXiv 2608.29595) does not mention the conjecture. The AlphaEvolve abstract (arXiv 2511.02864) does not either, though I did not read the full paper. The 'Claude' item in an aggregator (a claimed S^6 result) is unverified and unrelated, and I did not pursue it.
competing_reading: Read the two post-2024 items as progress that changes what a careful person would write. Fagan, Qiu and Wang prove the conjecture for a non-trivial class (every contractible cellular fake surface of complexity less than 6), and Dynnikov reduces the general case to standard polyhedra, so a 'partial progress' entry is arguable. The stronger reading is that neither changes the status. Fagan, Qiu and Wang's class is a strict subclass of the statement, and its Theorem 1 carries a hypothesis that the abstract omits. Its authors believe the conjecture false in general. Dynnikov proves a reduction, not an instance. On this reading the problem is still open, and the post-2024 activity is restricted-class work.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of arXiv 2608.23331 (Theorems 1.4, 1.5 and 2.5, whether Theorem 1.5 is new, and the definitions) and of arXiv 2412.12293 (Theorem 1 and Corollary 4, whether Corollary 4 carries the connected-1-skeleton hypothesis, a full scan for AI or computer-use statements), and v1 of 2412.12293 (whether Corollary 4 is already there). (2) A journal acceptance, or a review on zbMATH or MathSciNet, for either preprint. (3) The text of Matveev 1987 (both papers), Ikeda 1972, Gillman and Rolfsen 1983, and Cohen 1975, to fix the exact statements they prove and Cohen's exponent. (4) Later papers that cite the Fagan-Qiu-Wang or Dynnikov preprints and still call the conjecture open, or that settle it.

event.what_happened: L. Fagan, Y. Qiu and Z. Wang, 'Stable Andrews-Curtis Conjecture via Fake Surfaces and Zeeman Conjecture', arXiv:2412.12293. v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jan 2026 (the current version). The paper proposes an induction scheme for the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture (sACC), which is equivalent to 'every contractible fake surface is 3-deformable to a point'. Theorem 1 (v2): 'Contractible fake surfaces of complexity less than 6 with connected 1-skeletons are all 3-deformable to a point.' Corollary 4 (v2, Introduction): 'The Zeeman conjecture holds for any contractible cellular fake surface F of complexity less than 6.' The introduction also says: 'In the case of contractible fake surfaces that are not embeddable in 3-manifolds, the Zeeman conjecture is equivalent to sACC', and 'The Zeeman conjecture is believed to be false as well, but there are interesting special cases.' The v1 abstract, as fetched, makes no Zeeman claim (the title has 'Zeeman Conjecture'). Whether v1 already contains Corollary 4 is not verified.
event.revisions: v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jan 2026 (the current version). The changes between versions were not identified.
event.delivers: The conjecture for contractible cellular fake surfaces of complexity less than 6 (complexity read as vertex count, per the paper's ℱC(s,t) definition). A restricted class, not all contractible two-dimensional complexes. Also, per the authors, the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture for that complexity range.
event.remains: The conjecture for all contractible two-dimensional complexes outside that class: higher complexity, and complexes that are not fake surfaces. The stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture in general. Whether Corollary 4 carries the connected-1-skeleton hypothesis of Theorem 1 is not established.
event.time_since_posted: 22 months since v1 (Dec 2024); 9 months since v2 (Jan 2026)
event.directly_checkable: The objects are finite combinatorial complexes with at most five vertices, so the claims are finite checks in principle. Whether a computer check was used is not established from the sections I read; the paper says 'computer exploration has not yielded any new results so far'.
event.doubts: (1) Scope. The v2 abstract states the result without the connected-1-skeleton hypothesis that v2's Theorem 1 carries. Whether Corollary 4 inherits that hypothesis is not established from my reading. (2) The Zeeman claim is confined to cellular fake surfaces, while the conjecture concerns all finite contractible two-dimensional complexes. (3) The paper describes itself as 'an induction scheme that aims at establishing' sACC. Its proved part is the low-complexity case.
event.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture holding in the restricted class (the authors prove it there). The authors state that the Zeeman conjecture is 'believed to be false' in general, and that sACC is 'widely believed to be false'. That is their own belief, recorded here, not a verdict.

judgement.why: The statement is one universal question, so restricted-class proofs are cases. Fagan-Qiu-Wang 2024 (Corollary 4: the conjecture for contractible cellular fake surfaces of complexity < 6) is a case, unreviewed, after the snapshot. Dynnikov 2026 is mainly a reduction to standard polyhedra, which alone would be `none`, but its Theorem 1.5 asserts the conjecture for all polyhedra embeddable in 3-manifolds, which is a settled restriction, so it is a case. The Gemini credit there is language editing only, so its AI role is none. Andrews-Curtis papers (Shehper et al., Lisitsa, Zhang et al., Lackenby), the fake-surface classification, the higher-dimensional and I^q product results, and Popov's namesake embedding claim all answer different questions and are variants. The AI involvement in the Andrews-Curtis papers therefore never reaches this problem. The Gillman-Rolfsen and Matveev equivalences reduce the conjecture to other then-open conjectures, so they are none. Perelman's proof, combined with Gillman-Rolfsen, makes the standard-spine case true, so it is a pre-snapshot case.
judgement.doubts: Dynnikov's Theorem 1.5 may not be new (the talk abstract attributes the embeddable case to Gillman-Rolfsen plus Poincaré), and it was read only through a summariser. If it is not new, the event is purely a reduction (`none`). Fagan-Qiu-Wang's Corollary 4 may carry a connected-1-skeleton hypothesis that the abstract omits. Neither changes the tier: both events are a case either way, or Fagan-Qiu-Wang alone remains one.
